1.pericope_label: When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt
debates: Whether the verse is a prophecy of Christ
What the second calling is
Why the love is said to precede the birth
outliers: Ellicott denies that the words can be a prophecy of the Christ in this context, since obstinate conduct and rebellion would then be involved in the prediction, where Henry and Wesley both read a double aspect, the calling of Israel being a type of the calling of Christ
Calvin distinguishes two callings in the two verses, the first an actual liberation out of Egypt and the second the outward voice of teaching through the prophets
themes: A nation loved before it was born
A grave in Egypt with no spark of life
Prophets sent one after another and refused
A people who walked away as they were called

3.pericope_label: I taught Ephraim also to go, taking them by their arms; but they knew not that I healed them
debates: What the first word means
What the cords of a man are
What the raising of the yoke pictures
outliers: Calvin reports that the opening word occurs nowhere else in Scripture, canvasses whether it is a verb or a noun, and sides with those who make it a noun, since the alternative requires a change of letter at the beginning of a word for which no instance can be adduced

Ellicott turns the clause about not knowing into a charge against his own age, the refusal to own a divine origin for what blesses life being treated instead as the voice of nature or the development of humanity
themes: A child held up by both arms
Leading strings held at each end
A yoke lifted to let the air in
A bite of grass at the end of the furrow

5.pericope_label: He shall not return into the land of Egypt, but the Assyrian shall be his king, because they refused to return
debates: Whether the clauses are statements or questions
What the branches are
Why Egypt is closed to them
outliers: Ellicott takes both clauses of the verse as questions, shall he not return into the land of Egypt and shall not the Assyrian be his king, where Gill, Clarke and Calvin all read them as statements

Calvin prefers to read the second noun as the bolts of a gate rather than as branches, taking a part for the whole of the fortifications, while allowing the reading that makes them the towns and villages hanging on a city
themes: A refuge found shut when it is wanted
Men bound like beasts too fierce to be loosed
Bolts counted as the strength of a city
A sword that stayed until nothing was left

7.pericope_label: And my people are bent to backsliding from me: though they called them to the most High, none at all would exalt him
debates: What the word rendered backsliding means
Whether the people are bent or in suspense
Who is called and by whom
outliers: Clarke abandons the common rendering of the second clause for one that reads it of a yoke which will not be raised, tying the words back to the figure a few verses earlier
Ellicott notes that the verse drops the imagery of the chapter altogether and speaks in homely literal commonplace
themes: A bias that will not be corrected
A man hanging in the air, neither rising nor falling
Doubt kept up as an excuse
A call to the highest and a bent to the lowest

8.pericope_label: How shall I give thee up, Ephraim? how shall I deliver thee, Israel? how shall I make thee as Admah? how shall I set thee as Zeboim? mine heart is turned within me, my repentings are kindled together
debates: In what sense God can be said to deliberate or to repent
Whether the heart is turned within or against
Why Admah and Zeboim are named rather than the more famous cities
outliers: Ellicott alone abandons the received rendering of the last clause, reading the heart as turned against me rather than within me, and calling it a violent revulsion of feeling
Calvin turns the verse against those who would make God’s purpose wait upon human free will, holding that accommodation to our ignorance proves no change in God himself
themes: A father who cannot find it in his heart to disinherit
Cities of the plain named as a warning
A bow of promise on the darkest cloud
Justice pleading against mercy and losing

9.pericope_label: I will not execute the fierceness of mine anger, I will not return to destroy Ephraim: for I am God, and not man; the Holy One in the midst of thee: and I will not enter into the city
debates: What the refusal to return withholds
What it means not to enter into the city
Whether the comfort is offered to the whole nation or to a remnant
outliers: Ellicott sets aside the rendering of the ancient versions for one many commentators draw from the Hebrew, so that the clause promises not to come in wrath rather than not to enter a city
Calvin restricts the consolation to the faithful few, holding that the saying was never meant to relieve the sorrow of hypocrites
themes: A conqueror who does not come back to burn
Anger spoken of because we can hear it no other way
A shield held up against despair
A holy presence that stays inside the walls

10.pericope_label: They shall walk after the Lord: he shall roar like a lion: when he shall roar, then the children shall tremble from the west. They shall tremble as a bird out of Egypt, and as a dove out of the land of Assyria: and I will place them in their houses, saith the Lord
debates: Whether walking after the Lord is obedience or being led home
Whose voice the roaring is and whom it frightens
Whether the promise ends with the return from exile
outliers: Clarke dates the roar to a particular decree and makes the whole promise the return under Cyrus, down to the rebuilding of the temple and its ordinances
Calvin turns the birds around, applying the trembling not to the returning exiles but to the nations who would have stopped them
themes: A scattered body that has found its head again
A voice that carries to the ends of the earth
Doves flying home to their windows
A summons that frightens and gladdens at once

12.pericope_label: Ephraim compasseth me about with lies, and the house of Israel with deceit: but Judah yet ruleth with God, and is faithful with the saints
debates: Whether the verse belongs to this chapter at all
What being compassed about with lies pictures
Whether the second clause praises Judah or charges it
Who the saints are
outliers: Ellicott reverses the sense of the second clause, reading it that Judah roves unbridled rather than rules with God, and sets the inconstancy of Judah against the faithfulness of God
Calvin declines both the reading that takes the plural word for God himself and the reading that takes it for the sanctuary, calling the latter strained and without example
themes: A verse standing at the wrong side of a division
Falsehoods drawn up around God like a besieging army
A man who changes his ground each time he is caught
A kingdom whose crown and altar were given together
